questions.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}s,$ where $f(x,y,z)=x+y-z$ and the curve $C$ is parametrized by $r(t)=⟨{t}^{2}+1,\,{t}^{2}-1,\,{t}^{2}⟩$ for $t\in [0,2]?$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $r(t)=⟨{t}^{2}+1,\,{t}^{2}-1,\,{t}^{2}⟩,$ then along the curve we have $x={t}^{2}+1,$ $y={t}^{2}-1,$ and $z={t}^{2}.$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,k \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}+1)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-1)j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})k \\  & =2t\,i+2t\,j+2t\,k \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(2t)^{2}+(2t)^{2}+(2t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+4{t}^{2}+4{t}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{12{t}^{2}} \\  & =2\sqrt{3}|t| \\  & =2\sqrt{3}t\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $|t|=t$ since $t>0$ along the path of $C.$

Now, since $f(x,y,z)=x+y-z$, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =({t}^{2}+1)+({t}^{2}-1)-{t}^{2} \\  & =2{t}^{2}-{t}^{2} \\  & ={t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{2}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{t}^{2}\cdot 2\sqrt{3}t\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =2\sqrt{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}{t}^{3}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s,$ where $f(x,y)=\sqrt{2}(x-y)$ and the curve $C$ is parametrized 
 by $r(t)=⟨{t}^{2}+t,\,{t}^{2}-t⟩$ for $t\in [0,\sqrt{2}]?$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $r(t)=⟨{t}^{2}+t,\,{t}^{2}-t⟩,$ then along the curve we have $x={t}^{2}+t,$ and $y={t}^{2}-t.$ 

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}+t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-t)j \\  & =(2t+1)\,i+(2t-1)\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(2t+1)^{2}+(2t-1)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+4t+1+4{t}^{2}-4t+1} \\  & =\sqrt{8{t}^{2}+2} \\  & =\sqrt{2}\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+1}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, since $f(x,y)=\sqrt{2}(x-y)$, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\sqrt{2}[({t}^{2}+t)-({t}^{2}-t)] \\  & =2\sqrt{2}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}2\sqrt{2}t\cdot \sqrt{2}\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+1}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}t\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}z({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\,\text{d}s,$ where the curve $C$ is parametrized by $r(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j\,+t\,k$ for $\,0\le t\le \frac{\pi }{2}?$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $r(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j\,+t\,k,$ then along the curve we have $x=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,$ $y=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,$ and $z=t.$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,k \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)k \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j+k \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t+1} \\  & =\sqrt{1+1} \\  & =\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

  

Now, if $f(x,y,z)=z({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})$, then we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =t((\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}-(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}) \\  & =t({cos}^{2}⁡t-{sin}^{2}⁡t) \\  & =t\operatorname{cos}⁡2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as  

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}z({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}t\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\cdot \sqrt{2}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}t\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}\frac{x}{4y+1}\text{d}s,$ where the curve $C$ is parametrized by $r(t)=t\,i+{t}^{2}\,j\,$ for $0\le t\le 1?$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $r(t)=t\,i+{t}^{2}\,j,$ then along the curve we have $x=t$ and $y={t}^{2}.$ 

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})j \\  & =i+2tj \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+(2t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+4{t}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, if  $f(x,y)=\frac{x}{4y+1}$, then we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\frac{t}{4{t}^{2}+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\frac{x}{4y+1}\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(\frac{t}{4{t}^{2}+1})\cdot \sqrt{4{t}^{2}+1}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{t}{\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+1}}\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}s,$ where $f(x,y,z)=2x-{y}^{2}-{z}^{2}$ and the curve $C$ is parametrized by $r(t)=⟨{t}^{2},\,t-1,\,t+1⟩$ for $t\in [0,3]?$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $r(t)=⟨{t}^{2},\,t-1,\,t+1⟩,$ then along the curve we have $x={t}^{2},$ $y=t-1,$ and $z=t+1.$ 

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,k \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t-1)j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t+1)k \\  & =2t\,i+j+k \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(2t)^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+2}\end{aligned}
$$

  

Now, since $f(x,y,z)=2x-{y}^{2}-{z}^{2}$, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =2({t}^{2})-(t-1)^{2}-(t+1)^{2} \\  & =2{t}^{2}-({t}^{2}-2t+1)-({t}^{2}+2t+1) \\  & =2{t}^{2}-{t}^{2}+2t-1-{t}^{2}-2t-1 \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{3}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}(-2)\cdot \sqrt{4{t}^{2}+2}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}(-2)\cdot \sqrt{2(2{t}^{2}+1)}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}(-2)\cdot \sqrt{2}\cdot \sqrt{2{t}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =-2\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{3}\sqrt{2{t}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Evaluate the line integral of the function $f(x,y)=x+y$ along the curve $C$ parametrized by $r(t)=⟨t,\,1+t⟩$ for $t\in [0,1].$
questions.worked_solution:
To calculate the line integral, we will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Since $r(t)=⟨t,\,1+t⟩,$ then along the curve we have $x=t$ and $y=1+t.$    

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1+t)j \\  & =\,i+j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+1} \\  & =\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=x+y$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =t+(1+t)=2t+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(2t+1)\cdot \sqrt{2}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}2t+1\,\text{d}t \\  & =\sqrt{2}{[{t}^{2}+t]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\sqrt{2}(1+1-0) \\  & =2\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Evaluate the integral ${\int }_{C}({x}^{3}-2{y}^{3})\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the curve parametrized by $r(t)=4{t}^{2}\,i+3{t}^{2}\,j$ for $0\le t\le 1.$
questions.worked_solution:
To calculate the line integral, we will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Since $r(t)=4{t}^{2}\,i+3{t}^{2}\,j,$ then along the curve we have $x=4{t}^{2}$ and $y=3{t}^{2}.$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4{t}^{2})i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3{t}^{2})j \\  & =8t\,i+6t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(8t)^{2}+(6t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{64{t}^{2}+36{t}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{100{t}^{2}} \\  & =10|t| \\  & =10t.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $|t|=t$ since $t>0$ along the path of $C.$ 

Now, if $f(x,y)={x}^{3}-2{y}^{3}$, then we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & ={(4{t}^{2})}^{3}-2{(3{t}^{2})}^{3} \\  & ={4}^{3}{t}^{6}-2\cdot {3}^{3}{t}^{6} \\  & =64{t}^{6}-54{t}^{6} \\  & =10{t}^{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}({x}^{3}-{y}^{3})\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}10{t}^{6}\cdot 10t\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =100{\int }_{0}^{1}{t}^{7}\,\text{d}t \\  & =100\cdot \frac{{t}^{8}}{8}\,{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =100[\frac{{1}^{8}}{8}+\frac{{0}^{8}}{8}] \\  & =100\cdot \frac{1}{8} \\  & =12.5.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Evaluate the line integral of the function $f(x,y)=\frac{1}{y-x}$ along the curve $C$ parametrized by $r(t)=⟨t,\,t-4⟩$ for $t\in [0,4].$
questions.worked_solution:
To calculate the line integral, we will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Since $r(t)=⟨t,\,t-4⟩,$ then along the curve we have $x=t$ and $y=t-4.$     

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t-4)j \\  & =i+j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+1} \\  & =\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=\frac{1}{y-x}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\frac{1}{t-(4-t)}=-\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{4}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}-\frac{1}{4}\cdot \sqrt{2}\,\cdot \,\text{d}t \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}{\int }_{0}^{4}\text{d}t \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}t\,{|}_{0}^{4} \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}\cdot (4-0) \\  & =-\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Evaluate the integral ${\int }_{C}(2{x}^{2}-16)\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the curve parametrized by $r(t)=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j$ for $0\le t\le \frac{\pi }{4}.$
questions.worked_solution:
To calculate the line integral, we will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Since $r(t)=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,$ then along the curve we have $x=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t$ and $y=4\operatorname{sin}⁡t.$  

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{16{sin}^{2}⁡t+16{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{16({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =\sqrt{16} \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, if $f(x,y)=2{x}^{2}-16$, then we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =2(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}-16 \\  & =16(2{cos}^{2}⁡t-1) \\  & =16\operatorname{cos}⁡2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}(2{x}^{2}-16)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}16\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\cdot 4\,\text{d}t \\  & =64{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\,\text{d}t \\  & =64{[\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2t]}_{0}^{\pi /4} \\  & =32[\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-\operatorname{sin}⁡0] \\  & =32(1-0) \\  & =32.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Evaluate the integral ${\int }_{C}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the curve parametrized by $r(t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j$ for $0\le t\le \frac{\pi }{4}.$
questions.worked_solution:
To calculate the line integral, we will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Since $r(t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,$ then along the curve we have $x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t$ and $y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t.$  

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{sin}^{2}⁡t+4{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{4({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =\sqrt{4} \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, if $f(x,y)={y}^{2}$, then we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & ={(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}=4{sin}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}4{sin}^{2}⁡t\cdot 2\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =8{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =8{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}(\frac{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡2t}{2})\text{d}t \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡2t)\text{d}t \\  & =4{[t-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡2t}{2}]}_{0}^{\pi /4} \\  & =4[(\frac{\pi }{4}-\frac{1}{2})-0] \\  & =\pi -2.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Evaluate the line integral of the function $f(x,y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x$  along the curve $C$ parametrized by $r(t)={t}^{2}\,i-{t}^{2}\,j$ for $0<t<\sqrt{\pi /2}.$
questions.worked_solution:
To calculate the line integral, we will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Since $r(t)={t}^{2}\,i-{t}^{2}\,j,$ then along the curve we have $x={t}^{2}$ and $y=-{t}^{2}.$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-{t}^{2})\,j \\  & =2t\,j-2t\,k \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(2t)^{2}+(-2t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{8{t}^{2}} \\  & =2\sqrt{2}|t| \\  & =2\sqrt{2}t\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $|t|=t$ because $t>0$ along the path of $C.$

Now, since $f(x,y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{\pi /2}}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{\pi /2}}\operatorname{cos}⁡{t}^{2}\cdot 2\sqrt{2}\,t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u={t}^{2}$, $\text{d}u=2t\,\text{d}t$ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{\pi /2}}\operatorname{cos}⁡{t}^{2}\cdot 2\sqrt{2}\,t\,\text{d}t & =\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡u\,\,\text{d}u \\  & =\sqrt{2}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡u\,{|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\sqrt{2}(1-0) \\  & =\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Evaluate the line integral ${\int }_{C}\frac{y+z}{x}\,\text{d}s,$ where the curve $C$ is parametrized by $r(t)=t\,i+\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}\,j+\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}\,k$
for $1<t<\sqrt{2}.$
questions.worked_solution:
To calculate the line integral, we will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Since $r(t)=t\,i+\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}\,j+\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}\,k,$ then along the curve we have $x=t,$ $y=\frac{{t}^{2}}{2},$ and $z=\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}.$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,k \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{t}^{2}}{2})\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{t}^{2}}{2})\,k \\  & =i+t\,j+t\,k \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{t}^{2}+{t}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+2{t}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, if $f(x,y)=\frac{y+z}{x}$, then we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\frac{\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}+\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}}{t}=t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\frac{y+z}{x}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{1}^{\sqrt{2}}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{\sqrt{2}}t\sqrt{1+2{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=1+2{t}^{2}$, $\text{d}u=4t\,\text{d}t$ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{\sqrt{2}}t\sqrt{1+2{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{3}^{5}\sqrt{u}\cdot \frac{1}{4}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{3}^{5}{u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot \frac{2}{3}{u}^{3/2}\,{|}_{3}^{5} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}({5}^{3/2}-{3}^{3/2}) \\  & =\frac{5\sqrt{5}-3\sqrt{3}}{6}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Evaluate the line integral of the function $f(x,y)={x}^{3}+y$ along the curve parametrized by $r(t)=3t\,i+{t}^{3}\,j\,$ for $t\in [0,1].$
questions.worked_solution:
To calculate the line integral, we will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Since $r(t)=3t\,i+{t}^{3}\,j$, then along the curve we have $x=3t$ and $y={t}^{3}.$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3})\,j \\  & =3\,i+3{t}^{2}\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{3}^{2}+{(3{t}^{2})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{9+9{t}^{4}} \\  & =3\sqrt{1+{t}^{4}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)={x}^{3}+y$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(3t)^{3}+{t}^{3} \\  & =27{t}^{3}+{t}^{3} \\  & =28{t}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}28{t}^{3}\cdot 3\sqrt{1+{t}^{4}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}84{t}^{3}\sqrt{1+{t}^{4}}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=1+{t}^{4},$ $\text{d}u=4{t}^{3}\,\text{d}t$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}84{t}^{3}\sqrt{1+{t}^{4}}\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{1}^{2}21\cdot {u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =21\cdot \frac{2}{3}{u}^{3/2}{|}_{1}^{2} \\  & =14({2}^{3/2}-{1}^{3/2}) \\  & =14(2\sqrt{2}-1)\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Evaluate the line integral of the function $f(x,y)=\frac{12x}{y-1}$ along the curve parametrized by $r(t)={t}^{2}\,i+(t+1)\,j\,$ for $t\in [\sqrt{2},\sqrt{6}].$
questions.worked_solution:
To calculate the line integral, we will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Since $r(t)={t}^{2}\,i+(t+1)\,j$, then along the curve we have $x={t}^{2}$ and $y=t+1.$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t+1)\,j \\  & =2t\,i+j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(2t)^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=\frac{12x}{y-1}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\frac{12{t}^{2}}{(t+1)-1} \\  & =\frac{12{t}^{2}}{t} \\  & =12t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{\sqrt{2}}^{\sqrt{6}}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\sqrt{2}}^{\sqrt{6}}12t\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=4{t}^{2}+1,$ $\text{d}u=8t\,\text{d}t$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\sqrt{2}}^{\sqrt{6}}12t\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{9}^{25}\frac{3}{2}{u}^{1/2}\text{d}u \\  & ={u}^{3/2}{|}_{9}^{25} \\  & ={25}^{3/2}-{9}^{3/2} \\  & =125-27 \\  & =98\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Evaluate the line integral of the function $f(x,y)=\frac{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}{5},$ along the curve parametrized by $r(t)=⟨4\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩$ for $t\in [0,\frac{\pi }{2}].$
questions.worked_solution:
To calculate the line integral, we will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Since $r(t)=⟨4\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,$ then along the curve we have $x=4\operatorname{sin}⁡t$ and $y=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t.$   

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i-3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}+(-3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{16{cos}^{2}+9{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{25{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =5|\operatorname{cos}⁡t| \\  & =5\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $|\operatorname{cos}⁡t|=\operatorname{cos}⁡t$ because $\operatorname{cos}⁡t\ge 0$ when $t\in [0,\frac{\pi }{2}].$

Now, since $f(x,y)=\frac{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}{5}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\frac{16{sin}^{2}⁡t+9{sin}^{2}⁡t}{5} \\  & =\frac{25{sin}^{2}⁡t}{5} \\  & =5{sin}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}5{sin}^{2}⁡t\cdot 5\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =25{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{sin}^{2}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

   

We can solve this using the substitution $u=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,$ $\text{d}u=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t$ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}25{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{sin}^{2}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t & =25{\int }_{0}^{1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =25\cdot {\frac{{u}^{3}}{3}|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =25(\frac{1}{3}-0) \\  & =\frac{25}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Find an integral that is equivalent to $\displaystyle\int\limits_C xy^3 \, \textrm{d}s,$ where $C$ is the curve parametrized by $\mathbf r(t)= \left \langle \cos t, \sin t \right\rangle$ for $t \in \left(0, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14053150/assets/f53d78debfec5f8c50e0f3a5947d2a36126e18c073d7b0cc4c59d506753059b3.png)

The path of integration is shown above. We will use the formula

$$
\int\limits_C f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}s  = \int\limits_a^b  f(\mathbf r(t)) \, \| \mathbf r'(t) \| \, \textrm{d}t.
$$

 

Here, we have $f(x,y) =  xy^3$. Along the path, we have $x=\cos t$ and $y=\sin t,$ and so we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =f(\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot (\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{3} \\  & ={sin}^{3}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $\mathbf{r}'(t)$ and $\| \mathbf{r}'(t) \|,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}+{(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}x{y}^{3}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{sin}^{3}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot 1\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{sin}^{3}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we conclude that

$$
\int\limits_C xy^3 \, \textrm{d}s = \int^{\pi/2}_{0} \sin^3 t \cos t \, \textrm{d}t .
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Evaluate the integral $\displaystyle\int\limits_{C}xy\,\textrm{d}s,$ where $C$ is the curve parametrized by $\mathbf{r}(t) = 3t\,\mathbf{i}+4t\,\mathbf{j}\,$ for $0\leq t\leq 1.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To calculate the line integral, we will use the formula

$$
\int\limits_C f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}s  = \int\limits_a^b  f(\mathbf r(t)) \, \| \mathbf r'(t) \| \, \textrm{d}t.
$$

 

Since $\mathbf{r}(t) = 3t\,\mathbf{i}+4t\,\mathbf{j},$ then along the curve we have $x=3t$ and $y=4t.$

Computing $\mathbf{r}'(t)$ and $\| \mathbf{r}'(t) \|,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4t)j \\  & =3\,i+4\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{3}^{2}+{4}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{5}^{2}} \\  & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Now, if $f(x,y) =xy,$ then we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =3t\cdot 4t \\  & =12{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}xy\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}12{t}^{2}\cdot 5\,\text{d}t \\  & =60{\int }_{0}^{1}{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & =60{[\frac{{t}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =20{[{t}^{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =20.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Evaluate the line integral of $f(x,y,z) = \dfrac{x}{yz}$ along the curve parametrized by $\mathbf{r}(t) = t^2\, \mathbf{i} + t \,\mathbf{j} + 1 \,\mathbf{k}$ for $t \in [0,\sqrt 2].$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To calculate the line integral, we will use the formula

$$
\int\limits_C f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}s  = \int\limits_a^b  f(\mathbf r(t)) \, \| \mathbf r'(t) \| \, \textrm{d}t.
$$

 

Since $\mathbf{r}(t) =t^2\, \mathbf{i} + t \,\mathbf{j} + 1 \,\mathbf{k},$ then along the curve we have $x = t^2,$ $y = t,$ and $z=1.$  

Computing $\mathbf{r}'(t)$ and $\| \mathbf{r}'(t) \|,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,k \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1)\,k \\  & =2t\,i+1\,j+0\,k \\  & =2t\,i+j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(2t)^{2}+{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y,z) = \dfrac{x}{yz},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\frac{{t}^{2}}{t\cdot 1}=t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}t\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u= 4t^2+1,$ $\textrm d u=8t\,\textrm d t$ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}t\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{1}^{9}\frac{1}{8}{u}^{1/2}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{8}\cdot \frac{2}{3}{u}^{3/2}{|}_{1}^{9} \\  & =\frac{1}{12}[{9}^{3/2}-{1}^{3/2}] \\  & =\frac{1}{12}[27-1] \\  & =\frac{1}{12}\cdot 26 \\  & =\frac{13}{6}\end{aligned}
$$
